lines.line: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair.
lines.author: Charles Dickens
lines.what_its_doing: Dickens opens with the longest, most exhausting sentence he could write, and it works because the exhaustion is the point. He strings ten contradictions together using identical grammatical scaffolding, each one canceling the last, until the sentence collapses under its own weight. The repetition of 'it was' is rhythmic, almost liturgical, like a sermon or a legal document. The whole novel is going to operate this way: London against Paris, loyalty against betrayal, life against death, and the reader is placed inside that opposition before they even know what the story is.
lines.what_you_can_steal: If your book lives inside a contradiction, name both sides in the first sentence and let the tension between them do the work of a hook.

lines.line: Call me Ishmael.
lines.author: Herman Melville
lines.what_its_doing: Three words that every first-year creative writing student knows, and the effect is still almost impossible to replicate. The line gives you exactly one piece of information, which is what the narrator wants to be called. It withholds his real name, his origin, his reason for speaking. And the word 'Call' is doing most of the work, because it's imperative and it's also evasive. It sounds like an introduction and functions like a mask.
lines.what_you_can_steal: A single instruction sentence can carry more weight than a full paragraph of setup. Think about whether your first line can ask the reader to do something (trust me, watch this, listen) rather than tell them something.

lines.line: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
lines.author: Jane Austen
lines.what_its_doing: Austen opens with the most famous ironic statement in English literature. She says a single rich man must want a wife. Every sentence after this one will prove the opposite, which is that the women in the novel's world need the rich man, and the rich man is mostly a passive prize to be maneuvered over. The sentence is wrong on purpose, and the reader is invited to notice. By the time Mrs. Bennet starts scheming about Netherfield Park in paragraph three, you already know the narrator is laughing at her and at the entire economic system her scheming serves.
lines.what_you_can_steal: You can open with a statement the book will spend its length disproving. Irony in the first sentence sets up a contract between narrator and reader that pays off on every page after it.

lines.line: Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.
lines.author: Leo Tolstoy
lines.what_its_doing: Tolstoy opens with a philosophical claim, and the claim is wrong in the most interesting way. Happy families are not all alike, as anyone who has actually lived in a happy family knows, because happiness has as many textures as unhappiness does. But the wrongness is the point. The narrator is stating a folk wisdom that the novel will spend 800 pages dismantling. By opening with it, Tolstoy commits to a narrator who holds strong opinions about human nature, and invites the reader to hold the novel against that opinion for its entire length. Anna herself is introduced as proof that the claim about unhappiness is also wrong. Her unhappiness is borrowed, structured, inevitable, and it belongs entirely to her.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Open with a claim about human nature your book will spend its length complicating, and the tension between the claim and the evidence you present will carry readers forward on its own.

lines.line: It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.
lines.author: George Orwell
lines.what_its_doing: Orwell delivers a line that looks like straight description and contains exactly one impossible detail. 'A bright cold day in April' is exactly the kind of sentence anyone might write. Then the clocks strike thirteen. The reader has to stop. Clocks don't strike thirteen. The line doesn't announce dystopia or deliver a thesis statement. It simply places one detail that doesn't belong and trusts the reader to feel the wrongness. Every horror in the book works the same way: mundane surfaces, one detail that can't be right, and the dread that opens between them.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Bury your one impossible detail inside an otherwise normal description and let the reader find it themselves. Announced strangeness is cheap; discovered strangeness is what makes readers turn the page.

lines.line: Many years later, as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendía was to remember that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice.
lines.author: Gabriel García Márquez
lines.what_its_doing: García Márquez compresses three time periods into a single sentence, and he does it without any explanation. The colonel is about to die by firing squad. He's also remembering the afternoon his father showed him ice. We don't know when either event happens or how they connect, and we don't need to yet. The sentence commits to its own strangeness and trusts us to follow. By the second paragraph we're thirty years earlier and it feels natural, because the opening has already taught us the book's relationship to time.
lines.what_you_can_steal: A first line can establish the rules of time in your book. If you want non-linear storytelling to feel natural later, put a time-jump in sentence one and refuse to apologize for it.

lines.line: Mother died today.
lines.author: Albert Camus
lines.what_its_doing: Two words and a subject. 'Mother died today.' Meursault doesn't write 'My mother died today.' The possessive is gone, and so is every marker of grief. He reports it the way you'd report a train time. The line's genius is in what it withholds: no emotion, no context, no softening. Camus puts the existentialist thesis on the first line and then spends the rest of the novel building the circumstances that will punish Meursault for it. The detachment is the entire argument of the book, compressed to five syllables.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Strip every softening word from your first sentence and see if the rawness of what's left is itself the hook. Sometimes the most powerful thing is what the narrator refuses to feel.

lines.line: It was a queer, sultry summer, the summer they electrocuted the Rosenbergs, and I didn't know what I was doing in New York.
lines.author: Sylvia Plath
lines.what_its_doing: Plath starts with a weather description, pivots to an execution, and lands on a young woman who doesn't know what she's doing. The Rosenbergs are executed in the same breath as the heat, as though they're part of the atmosphere, part of the summer's oppressiveness. The technique here is juxtaposition: private confusion sitting inside public catastrophe, neither one explaining the other. By the time you've read the sentence twice, you understand that the narrator's disorientation is as large and as real as the political climate she's living inside. The whole novel operates this way, the personal and the historical pressing against each other, neither giving way.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Put your character's interior confusion against a specific historical or public event in the same breath, and let the reader feel how much the outside world is pressing on your protagonist's private crisis.

lines.line: Lolita, light of my life, fire of my loins.
lines.author: Vladimir Nabokov
lines.what_its_doing: Nabokov opens on pure music. 'Lolita, light of my life, fire of my loins.' The alliteration is gorgeous, the L's and the F's, the way 'life' and 'loins' rhyme. And that's the trap. The sentence is designed to seduce the reader the same way Humbert tries to seduce everyone around him: aesthetically, through sheer beauty of language. By the time you register what 'fire of my loins' actually means about this man's obsession, you're already inside the music. The whole novel is a defense brief written in the most beautiful prose imaginable, and this is the opening argument.
lines.what_you_can_steal: If your narrator is unreliable or morally compromised, make the prose itself complicit in the seduction. Beautiful language that carries ugly meaning is more disturbing than ugly language that announces it.

lines.line: As Gregor Samsa awoke one morning from uneasy dreams he found himself transformed in his bed into a gigantic insect.
lines.author: Franz Kafka
lines.what_its_doing: Kafka doesn't reveal, explain, or foreshadow. Gregor woke up as an insect. Present tense of fact. The sentence reports the transformation the same way you'd report waking up late, and that matter-of-factness is where the horror lives. The book never explains why it happened, and the first line sets that contract with the reader: this is a world where giant insects happen, and we're going to discuss what it means for the family's finances. The existential nightmare is in the fact that everyone just... continues to have practical concerns about it.
lines.what_you_can_steal: State your impossible premise in plain declarative language, with no hedging and no explanation, and the reader will take it seriously precisely because you do.

lines.line: In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I've been turning over in my mind ever since.
lines.author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
lines.what_its_doing: Nick Carraway introduces himself by giving us his father's advice, not his own biography. It's an evasion dressed as an opening. He's telling us he's reserved, that he learned reserve as a child, that he came to New York with a moral posture he's been carrying a long time. 'Younger and more vulnerable' tells us he's older now and less vulnerable, which means something happened to harden him. The line creates a Nick who is already looking back at a completed story, and it tells us that the advice, whatever it was, got tested and probably failed. The whole novel is a retrospective told by someone trying to maintain a moral position that the events he's describing have made impossible to hold.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Put your first-person narrator at a remove from the events of the book by opening with a memory or a lesson learned, and the reader will immediately understand that something is being processed, not merely reported.

lines.line: If you really want to hear about it, the first thing you'll probably want to know is where I was born, and what my lousy childhood was like, and how my parents were occupied and all before they had me, and all that David Copperfield kind of crap, but I don't feel like going into it, if you want to know the truth.
lines.author: J.D. Salinger
lines.what_its_doing: Salinger opens with Holden refusing to do the thing an opening is supposed to do. He knows the convention, 'where I was born, and what my lousy childhood was like,' and he names it, dismisses it, and then keeps talking anyway. The meta-awareness of the form is what makes this such a radical line in 1951. Holden is defining himself in opposition to the novel that hasn't started yet. The hostility, the casual profanity ('David Copperfield kind of crap'), the qualification 'if you want to know the truth' are all character in motion before the story exists. The book is the voice. There's no story separate from the way Holden tells it.
lines.what_you_can_steal: If your narrator has a voice strong enough to carry a book, let the first sentence demonstrate that voice at its most concentrated and combative. The reader should know exactly who they're dealing with before they know anything else.

lines.line: 124 was spiteful.
lines.author: Toni Morrison
lines.what_its_doing: Three words that treat a house as a character. Morrison doesn't write 'The house at 124 was haunted' or 'Something was wrong with the house.' She writes '124 was spiteful,' as though the house has a personality, a grudge, an intention. The choice to use the number instead of 'the house' or an address collapses the distance between the reader and the place. You're inside the thing before you know what it is. The whole novel is going to work this way, with the supernatural treated as ordinary and the ordinary treated as supernatural.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Personify your setting. If your story is rooted in a specific place, give the place an attitude in sentence one. The reader will treat it as a character for the rest of the book.

lines.line: When he woke in the woods in the dark and the cold of the night he'd reach out to touch the child sleeping beside him.
lines.author: Cormac McCarthy
lines.what_its_doing: McCarthy drops you inside a habitual action. 'When he woke' signals a pattern of mornings, not a specific one. He reaches for the child before he's even fully conscious, which tells you everything about the man's psychology and the world he's living in. The syntax is plain, stripped of quotation marks and commas, in the style McCarthy uses throughout the book. The line describes a father's reflex, not the apocalypse. The tenderness in 'reach out to touch' against the darkness of 'in the woods in the dark and the cold of the night' creates the tension that the entire novel will live inside: love persisting inside conditions designed to destroy it.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Start in a habitual action rather than a one-time event. A repeated gesture reveals character more efficiently than any single dramatic moment, and it tells the reader immediately what kind of story they're in.

lines.line: You are about to begin reading Italo Calvino's new novel, If on a winter's night a traveler.
lines.book: If on a winter's night a traveler
lines.author: Italo Calvino
lines.what_its_doing: Calvino opens by naming the reader, naming himself, and naming the book they're both holding. The second-person address turns reading into a performance. 'You are about to begin reading' means you are doing it right now, as you read those words. It's a trick, and it's an announcement that tricks are the subject. The sentence makes the act of reading the content of the book before any story has started. Calvino will spend the next 200 pages dismantling and reassembling the experience of fiction, and the first sentence tells you exactly what the experiment is: you're going to read about reading.
lines.what_you_can_steal: If your book is formally experimental, the first sentence should perform the experiment. Don't describe what the book will do. Do it, in sentence one.

lines.line: Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again.
lines.author: Daphne du Maurier
lines.what_its_doing: Du Maurier opens in the conditional past. 'I dreamt I went' puts us inside a memory of a dream, twice removed from anything real. We don't know who the narrator is, where she is now, or why she's dreaming of Manderley. The 'again' is doing critical work: it tells us she's been there before, that she's been away, that she returns in dreams even when she can't return in life. The sentence sets up loss, obsession, and a location charged with everything the narrator can't have. Manderley becomes the book's central character in that first line, before we've seen a single room of it.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Name your book's most important location in the first sentence and give it the weight of a person by showing what it means to your narrator to be away from it.

lines.line: It was a pleasure to burn.
lines.author: Ray Bradbury
lines.what_its_doing: Bradbury gives you a pleasure that has no object. Burning what? He doesn't say. The line commits fully to Montag's interiority and refuses to explain the context, which makes it more intimate and more disturbing than any description of a burning building could be. 'It was a pleasure' sounds like the opening of a love story, the words gentle, personal, almost domestic. Then the subject arrives and it's incineration. The whole novel is about the seductiveness of destruction, about how societies learn to love what's killing them, and Bradbury announces that argument in four words.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Open with your character's emotional relationship to an action rather than the action itself, and let the reader discover the action from inside the feeling. The dissonance between tone and content is the hook.

lines.line: The studio was filled with the rich odour of roses, and when the light summer wind stirred amidst the trees of the garden, there came through the open door the heavy scent of the lilac, or the more delicate perfume of the pink-flowering thorn.
lines.author: Oscar Wilde
lines.what_its_doing: Wilde opens inside sensation rather than action. The studio is full of rose odor, the wind is moving through the garden, the lilac and thorn come through the open door. Before any character appears, the reader is placed inside a specific sensory experience, heavy, layered, almost too sweet. The sentence is building toward the aesthetic argument at the center of the novel: that beauty is sufficient justification for anything. Lord Henry will articulate this later in dialogue, but Wilde embeds it in the prose itself before any character speaks. This is a book that believes in surfaces, and the surface of sentence one is gorgeous enough to make you half-believe it too.
lines.what_you_can_steal: If your novel has a philosophical argument, let the prose itself make that argument before any character does. The reader who's already been seduced by a beautiful opening has already agreed, partly, to the book's terms.

lines.line: 3 May. Bistritz. Left Munich at 8:35 p.m. on 1st May, arriving at Vienna early next morning; should have arrived at 6:46, but train was an hour late.
lines.author: Bram Stoker
lines.what_its_doing: Stoker opens as a travel diary: date, location, departure time, arrival time, and a train that was an hour late. The banality is strategic. Jonathan Harker is a solicitor's clerk, meticulous, rational, a man who records train schedules because that's the kind of man he is. Every entry in this first section of the book sounds exactly like a dutiful professional doing exactly what a dutiful professional does. The contrast between that voice and what that voice is eventually forced to describe creates the novel's central horror: an orderly, modern man confronting something his orderly, modern mind has no category for. The mundane opening is the setup for everything the supernatural is going to do to it.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Match your opening voice to your protagonist's psychology, not to the genre of the book. A horror novel can open in a bureaucratic voice if the protagonist is a bureaucrat, and the contrast between that voice and the horrors it will eventually have to record is the real engine.

lines.line: You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings.
lines.author: Mary Shelley
lines.what_its_doing: Shelley opens mid-correspondence and mid-reassurance. Walton is writing to his sister, heading toward the North Pole, telling her not to worry. 'You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings.' The formality of the sentence, the legal weight of 'enterprise,' the 'evil forebodings' that someone has already expressed: it's all foreshadowing built into the form of reassurance. The reader knows that a letter opener of 'don't worry' is a promise the book intends to break. Shelley also introduces the frame structure in the first word, because this is a letter inside a story inside a frame, and all the nested voices are part of how the novel interrogates who gets to tell the story of creation gone wrong.
lines.what_you_can_steal: If you need an epistolary opener, make the reassurance the foreboding. A character insisting nothing has gone wrong tells the reader that something is very wrong, and the dramatic irony sets up every page that follows.

lines.line: Someone must have slandered Josef K., for one morning, without having done anything truly wrong, he was arrested.
lines.author: Franz Kafka
lines.what_its_doing: Kafka opens with passive voice and an unknown accuser, and that grammatical choice is the whole argument. 'Someone must have slandered' rather than 'someone slandered,' because we're not sure, we can only infer. The uncertainty is baked into the sentence structure. Josef K. has been arrested for doing nothing wrong, by someone, for reasons no one will ever specify, and this sentence models exactly the experience Kafka is about to put him through. The logic is circular and bureaucratic before the first scene begins. The reader doesn't need to be told that the justice system in this novel is opaque and irrational. The opener is written in its grammar.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Let your sentence structure enact your theme. If your book is about a system of control or bureaucracy, write in passive voice and watch how quickly the reader feels the oppression without being told about it.

lines.line: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
lines.author: Virginia Woolf
lines.what_its_doing: Woolf opens in the middle of a decision. Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself. She's already said it, we've missed the moment, we're catching up, we're already inside her day. The 'herself' is the key word. It implies someone else usually does it, which implies servants, money, a certain class position. It implies insistence, that she wants to do this personally, which implies something is going on with wanting to be out, to be moving, to be in the world rather than in the house. The stream of consciousness that will follow for 200 pages is announced in one sentence: we're inside a mind that makes small decisions charged with personal meaning.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Put your first-person or close-third narrator in the middle of a small, charged decision rather than a dramatic event, and the reader will lean in to understand what the decision means to the person making it.

lines.line: "Yes, of course, if it's fine tomorrow," said Mrs Ramsay.
lines.author: Virginia Woolf
lines.what_its_doing: Woolf opens with dialogue and a condition. 'If it's fine tomorrow' is a qualified yes to something we haven't heard asked. The speech is attributed before we know who Mrs. Ramsay is, and we're already in the middle of a conversation between her and a child who wants to go to the lighthouse. We don't know that yet. We're in the response, inside the family's internal weather before the literal weather has been established. The whole novel is going to work this way: around the edges of things, through implications and conditional statements, never landing on the event directly. The lighthouse trip hangs over the first part of the novel as a promise, and 'if it's fine' is already the first equivocation.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Open in the middle of dialogue, with a response before we've heard the question, and the reader will spend the first pages filling in what they've missed, which means they're already invested in reconstructing the scene.

lines.line: Through the fence, between the curling flower spaces, I could see them hitting.
lines.author: William Faulkner
lines.what_its_doing: Faulkner opens in Benjy's perception, and Benjy's perception is limited in ways the reader can't yet understand. Through the fence, between spaces, he sees people hitting something. Golfers, as it turns out, but we won't know that for pages. The 'curling flower spaces' is Benjy processing the pattern in the wire fence, which is not how a person with typical cognition describes a fence. The first sentence establishes the POV without explaining it, which means the reader is immediately doing interpretive work, working out who this voice belongs to and what its limitations are. The whole first section of the novel operates on that interpretive pressure, and this line is where it starts.
lines.what_you_can_steal: If your narrator has unusual perceptual limits or a non-standard consciousness, demonstrate those limits in the first sentence without explaining them. Let the reader deduce the filter. The deduction itself creates engagement.

lines.line: Ships at a distance have every man's wish on board.
lines.author: Zora Neale Hurston
lines.what_its_doing: Hurston opens with an image rather than a character or an action. Ships at a distance carry men's wishes, and every man watches those ships differently depending on who he is. The second sentence, which follows immediately, tells us that women forget about their ships entirely and forget they've forgotten. It's a meditation on desire and resignation before Janie has been introduced by name. Hurston is setting the thematic premise, that women's inner lives are treated as expendable by the culture around them, as a piece of compressed social observation rather than argument. When Janie walks into the novel a paragraph later, returning from somewhere she refused to forget, the reader already knows what her return means.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Open with a small philosophical observation that your protagonist's story will prove or disprove, and place your character inside that frame when they arrive so the reader immediately understands the stakes of their specific life.

lines.line: I am an invisible man.
lines.author: Ralph Ellison
lines.what_its_doing: Ellison opens with a declaration and an immediate complication. 'I am an invisible man.' The next two sentences clarify that he's not talking about a horror story or a physics experiment. People simply refuse to see him. The power of 'I am' is that it's an assertion of existence, and existence is exactly what's being contested. The narrator is insisting on his own reality in the first words of a novel about a society that systematically denies that reality. The irony compounds across the book: the more forcefully he declares himself, the more the world proves his invisibility. The whole novel lives in the gap between 'I am' and 'you don't see me.'
lines.what_you_can_steal: If your book is about a character whose humanity is denied by the world around them, open with an affirmation of that humanity so flat and direct that its contradiction becomes the engine of everything that follows.

lines.line: All this happened, more or less.
lines.author: Kurt Vonnegut
lines.what_its_doing: Vonnegut opens the novel before the novel starts and tells you immediately that you can't trust the account you're about to receive. 'All this happened, more or less.' The 'more or less' is doing everything: it signals an unreliable narrator, a traumatized consciousness, a book that will mix the real and the invented without apology. It's also the closest thing to honesty Vonnegut can manage about Dresden, which he's spent 23 years trying to write and couldn't write straight. The admission of imprecision is the most precise thing he could say. The whole novel operates from that position: semi-true, semi-invented, exactly like memory, and especially like the memory of trauma.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Build your narrator's unreliability directly into the first sentence with a qualifier that acknowledges the account is imperfect, and the reader will trust the imperfection more than they'd trust a clean official version.

lines.line: Marley was dead: to begin with.
lines.author: Charles Dickens
lines.what_its_doing: Dickens opens with a death and then immediately undercuts it with the strangest four words in Victorian fiction: 'to begin with.' The construction is casual, almost breezy, as though the narrator is settling in for a long explanation before getting to the real point. And that's exactly the move. The death of Marley matters because it's the precondition for Scrooge's haunting, and Dickens can't let you spend five minutes doubting that Marley is actually gone. So he locks down the fact of the death in sentence one and then signals, with that aside, that there's much more to come. The whole novel runs on this voice: a knowing narrator who has already seen how the story ends and finds the telling of it slightly amusing.
lines.what_you_can_steal: If your story requires the reader to accept a premise before it can function, establish that premise in sentence one and use voice to signal you're doing it on purpose. The confidence of the delivery is what makes the reader trust you.

lines.line: A squat grey building of only thirty-four stories.
lines.author: Aldous Huxley
lines.what_its_doing: It's a fragment. No verb. Just a building, described in four adjectives that all carry the same grey bureaucratic weight, followed by a qualifying phrase that turns the building's size into its own kind of irony. 'Only thirty-four stories' is doing the heavy lifting, because in our world thirty-four stories is enormous, but in this world it's nothing. Huxley establishes the scale of the civilization before he establishes anything else, and he does it without a single human character in frame. The opening chapter of Brave New World will go on to describe a factory that produces human beings, and the fragment structure of the first sentence already feels like a lab report. Flat, observational, slightly inhuman.
lines.what_you_can_steal: A fragment as your first sentence isn't a gimmick if it's doing structural work. It can establish the register of an entire narrative, telling the reader whether they're in a character's head or watching from a clinical distance.

lines.line: Jack Torrance thought: Officious little prick.
lines.author: Stephen King
lines.what_its_doing: King gives you the thought before he gives you the thinker, and the thought is an insult. You don't know who Jack Torrance is, but you know he's thinking 'Officious little prick' about someone in the first line, which tells you more about Jack than three paragraphs of backstory would. The free indirect style is instant and total, and you're inside his skull before the novel has announced itself. And the choice of that particular phrase matters: it's the exact language of a man who's used to being the smartest person in the room and deeply, chronically resents authority he doesn't respect. The whole arc of Jack's breakdown is already encoded in that first insult. He's the kind of man who would think something like that about a hotel manager he just met, and then smile and shake the manager's hand.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Opening with a character's internal voice before naming them forces intimacy. The reader bonds with the perspective before forming any judgment about the person holding it.

lines.line: The North Carolina Mutual Life Insurance agent promised to fly from Mercy to the other side of Lake Superior at three o'clock.
lines.author: Toni Morrison
lines.what_its_doing: Morrison front-loads specificity so dense it almost resists entry: a named insurance company, a named hospital, a named lake, a specific time. On first read it sounds like a news story. But then you hit the content of what the sentence is actually reporting, which is a man promising to fly. No metaphor. He has announced, publicly, that he will step off a roof and fly across Lake Superior at three in the afternoon. Morrison holds these two registers in the same sentence: the bureaucratic precision of a local notice and the mythic impossibility of human flight. The whole novel is going to do this. Magic and mundane, held together without any flag for which is which, until you stop needing the flag.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Grounding the impossible in institutional specifics (a name, a time, a place) makes readers receive the impossible as simply another fact, which is the only way magic realism actually works.

lines.line: He was an old man who fished alone in a skiff in the Gulf Stream and he had gone eighty-four days now without taking a fish.
lines.book: The Old Man and the Sea
lines.author: Ernest Hemingway
lines.what_its_doing: Hemingway sets up failure as the character's defining condition before he sets up anything else. Eighty-four days without a fish. The number is specific and the specificity is brutal. It's not 'a long time,' it's eighty-four actual days, which is almost three months of daily failure. The sentence also establishes the isolation ('alone in a skiff') and the setting without making a production of either. What it does most efficiently is answer the first question any reader has about a character: what are they up against? The old man is up against a streak of loss that would have broken most men, and the first sentence tells you that and nothing else. The book will then make you watch him fail again, on a larger scale, and call it something other than failure.
lines.what_you_can_steal: State your character's defining problem in the first sentence, and make it specific enough that the reader understands the weight of it before they know anything else about the person carrying it.

lines.line: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit.
lines.author: J.R.R. Tolkien
lines.what_its_doing: The sentence does three things in eight words. It establishes a setting (a hole in the ground), introduces an unexplained creature (a hobbit), and implies by the matter-of-fact phrasing that this is completely normal. The word 'hobbit' is invented and Tolkien doesn't explain it. He just uses it as though you already know, which creates instant world-mythology, the sense that hobbits existed before this sentence and will exist after the story ends. Children's literature often opens by reassuring the reader that they're in good hands. Tolkien does the opposite: he drops you into a world mid-existence and trusts the strangeness to be magnetic rather than confusing.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Introduce your invented term or creature as though it requires no explanation, and the reader will accept it as a fact of the world rather than a construct of the author.

lines.line: It was night again.
lines.author: Patrick Rothfuss
lines.what_its_doing: Four words, and the most interesting of them is 'again.' The word implies repetition, a return, a cycle of nights that have already happened and will keep happening. It places the reader in medias res without any action, just a mood, a state, a recurring condition. Rothfuss opens The Name of the Wind with a chapter about silence, about a legendary man hiding in a small-town inn, and 'It was night again' is the exact right first sentence for that chapter: quiet, cyclical, carrying the weight of all the nights before this one. By page five you understand that Kvothe has been hiding for a long time. The first sentence already knew that.
lines.what_you_can_steal: A single word implying repetition ('again,' 'still,' 'another') can load a first sentence with history before the story has technically begun.

lines.line: In the week before their departure to Arrakis, when all the final scurrying about had reached a nearly unbearable frenzy, an old crone came to visit the mother of the boy, Paul.
lines.author: Frank Herbert
lines.what_its_doing: Herbert embeds four story elements in one sentence (a departure, a destination, a family under pressure, and an unexpected visitor) and wraps them in a frame that emphasizes chaos ('nearly unbearable frenzy') against the intrusion of something ancient and strange ('an old crone'). The construction delays the visitor until the very end of the sentence, which is correct, because the crone is the point. Everything before her is context for why she matters: the family is about to leave everything behind, they're overwhelmed, they're vulnerable. Into that vulnerability walks something that the novel will later reveal as a test older than the family's civilization. The first sentence sets up an action-thriller opening (departure, stakes, urgency) and then bends it toward myth in the final clause.
lines.what_you_can_steal: If your inciting event involves an intrusion into an already-stressed situation, structure your first sentence so the intrusion lands last, after the reader has already absorbed the pressure the character is under.

lines.line: The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel.
lines.author: William Gibson
lines.what_its_doing: Gibson doesn't describe the sky. He gives you a comparison that tells you there's no sky left to describe. 'The color of television, tuned to a dead channel' was written in 1984, when a dead channel meant static grey noise, and it's still the most accurate description of a sky that's been chemically or industrially destroyed. The simile works by importing a domestic failure, a television that's receiving nothing, into a natural space where it has no business being, and the displacement is the point. This world is so thoroughly mediated by technology that nature can only be described through broken machines. That's the whole thesis of cyberpunk, delivered in a single image, before the novel has introduced a character.
lines.what_you_can_steal: A simile that imports one domain into another (technology into nature, the domestic into the violent, the mundane into the mythic) can do more world-building work than a paragraph of exposition.

lines.line: My name is Kathy H.
lines.author: Kazuo Ishiguro
lines.what_its_doing: The initial reads as one of the plainest first sentences in literary fiction. A name, an initial for a last name that won't be given. That truncation is doing everything. The 'H.' is a half-withholding, the first in a novel entirely structured around what is withheld and when, about what Kathy knows and when she lets the reader know it. Ishiguro has built an entire book on the reader slowly realizing what Kathy is, what Hailsham was, what the 'donation' euphemism means. The flat conversational register of 'My name is Kathy H.' establishes the narrator's characteristic mode: calm, ordinary, slightly evasive. She'll tell you everything, but in her own order, and the order is designed to delay the full horror as long as possible.
lines.what_you_can_steal: When your narrator has something to hide, let the first sentence model the evasion. A name withheld, a word avoided, a phrasing slightly too careful: the reader's instinct toward the gap begins on page one.

lines.line: We slept in what had once been the gymnasium.
lines.author: Margaret Atwood
lines.what_its_doing: Atwood opens on displacement. 'What had once been the gymnasium' tells you this is a place repurposed, a world reorganized, a past tense sitting inside a present condition. The narrator is sleeping in a gymnasium with other people, and she doesn't explain why, and the past tense reference to what the room once was signals that she knows the difference. She remembers the before. The whole novel is a before-and-after structure, memory of a lost world set against the brutal present of Gilead, and the first sentence introduces that structure immediately. The gymnasium also does something specific: it's a young woman's space, a school space, a place of health and movement, turned into a dormitory for people with no freedom of movement. The irony is load-bearing.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Open with a present location described in terms of its former identity and you get displacement, loss, and worldbuilding in the same sentence, without any character having to explain what changed or why.

lines.line: The snow in the mountains was melting and Bunny had been dead for several weeks before we came to understand the gravity of our situation.
lines.author: Donna Tartt
lines.what_its_doing: Tartt opens with the rarest first-sentence move in crime fiction: she tells you there's a body before she tells you anything else, and she names the dead man casually, as though he's been dead long enough that his name is just a name now. The sentence also does something that the genre almost never does, which is to confess complicity in the first line. 'We came to understand the gravity of our situation' is a narrator talking about themselves as part of a group that has done something. The murder is already solved. The mystery Tartt is actually writing is psychological: how do a group of people who think of themselves as exceptional end up here? The snow melting beside Bunny's death is not incidental. The natural world is moving on, indifferent, while the characters still haven't absorbed what they've done.
lines.what_you_can_steal: In crime fiction, telling the reader who died in sentence one and framing it through the murderer's dawning awareness removes whodunit suspense entirely and replaces it with the more interesting question of how people live with what they've done.

lines.line: When I think of my wife, I always think of her head.
lines.author: Gillian Flynn
lines.what_its_doing: Flynn gives you a husband thinking about his wife's head, and the image is both tender and menacing at the same time. 'When I think of my wife' sounds like the opening of a love story. 'I always think of her head' sounds like the opening of a murder mystery. You can't tell yet which book you're in, and that's the point. The whole novel is about a marriage where both spouses are lying about which kind of book they're in, and the first sentence tells you that's going to be the game.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Write a first line with two equally valid readings, one safe and one dangerous. The reader's uncertainty about which interpretation is correct is the pull that drags them into sentence two.

lines.line: She's buried beneath a silver birch tree, down towards the old train tracks, her grave marked with a cairn.
lines.author: Paula Hawkins
lines.what_its_doing: The first sentence describes a grave. You don't know whose. You don't know who's speaking or how they know this. Hawkins puts you in a position of ignorance that's different from suspense. You're not waiting for a threat, you're already past the threat, standing at its conclusion. The cairn marking the grave is a specific detail, an image that suggests both informality (no headstone, no official marker) and care (someone placed stones). Someone is buried near train tracks under a birch tree in the kind of unmarked way that suggests the burial wasn't official. The narrator knows where the body is. That knowledge is the foundation of the entire unreliable-narrator structure that follows.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Starting at the aftermath of a crime rather than the crime itself puts the reader in a position of retrospective awareness that generates immediate questions about how things got to this point, which is often more compelling than watching the event unfold in real time.

lines.line: Renowned curator Jacques Saunière staggered through the vaulted archway of the museum's Grand Gallery.
lines.author: Dan Brown
lines.what_its_doing: Brown front-loads a reputation ('renowned curator'), a name, and an action ('staggered') in that order, and the action immediately contradicts the reputation. A renowned curator doesn't stagger. The word is undignified, physical, urgent, and it signals that something has already gone very wrong before the sentence ends. Brown is doing pure thriller mechanics: introduce status, immediately threaten it. The 'Grand Gallery' establishes the Louvre without naming it, and the compound noun 'vaulted archway' places you in European institutional grandeur. He's set up the whole first chapter in twenty words: a dying man in a museum, alone, with something he needs to communicate before he's gone. It's efficient in the way airport thrillers have to be efficient.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Naming a character's status and then immediately showing it compromised (staggered, bleeding, cornered, running) creates a gap between who this person is and what's happening to them, and that gap is where thriller tension lives.

lines.line: It happened every year, was almost a ritual.
lines.book: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo
lines.author: Stieg Larsson
lines.what_its_doing: Larsson opens on ritual, which is the right word because the novel is ultimately about inherited obsession. 'It happened every year' places you inside a recurring event without telling you what the event is, and the phrase 'was almost a ritual' clarifies that whoever is at the center of this recurring event has treated it as sacred. The withholding is calculated: you know the cadence but not the content. The novel opens this way because it needs to establish an old man's decades-long grief before it can make you understand why he would hire a disgraced journalist to investigate a forty-year-old disappearance. The ritual framing also signals that this story is about the past, about things that keep happening long after they should have stopped.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Opening on a recurring event, a ritual or an annual occurrence the character treats as fixed, implies the weight of all the previous times before the story has shown you even one of them.

lines.line: Mr. and Mrs. Dursley, of number four, Privet Drive, were proud to say that they were perfectly normal, thank you very much.
lines.book: Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone
lines.author: J.K. Rowling
lines.what_its_doing: Rowling does something quietly sophisticated with 'proud to say that they were perfectly normal, thank you very much.' The 'thank you very much' is the key. It's defensive, pre-emptive, slightly indignant, the phrasing of someone who expects to be contradicted. People who are actually normal don't feel the need to announce it, and they certainly don't add 'thank you very much' to the announcement. The sentence introduces the Dursleys as people in active denial of something they don't want to name, and it does this through voice rather than exposition. The whole book is structured around the collision between the Dursley world (ordinary, repressive, proud of its ordinariness) and the wizarding world they're trying to keep Harry away from. The tension between those two worlds starts in the first sentence.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Let a character's self-description reveal their defensiveness ('proud to say,' 'I've always believed,' 'not that it matters') and the reader will intuit what they're hiding before you've written a word of backstory.

lines.line: Far out in the uncharted backwaters of the unfashionable end of the western spiral arm of the Galaxy lies a small unregarded yellow sun.
lines.book: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
lines.author: Douglas Adams
lines.what_its_doing: Adams spends thirty-two words getting you to Earth, and by the time you arrive it's been called uncharted, backwater, unfashionable, and unregarded. The comic effect depends on the escalating accumulation of diminishment, each word making the destination smaller and less important, and the technique is also doing genuine worldbuilding. The narrator's perspective is cosmic and slightly contemptuous of scale, which is the exact perspective needed for a novel in which Earth is demolished to make way for a hyperspace bypass. The anthropocentric assumption (that Earth matters, that humans are central) is demolished before the novel starts, in the first sentence. Everything after that is the characters catching up to what the narrator already knows.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Establishing your narrator's relationship to scale in the first sentence, whether they find human concerns enormous or negligible, sets the reader's orientation for everything that follows.

lines.line: No live organism can continue for long to exist sanely under conditions of absolute reality; even larks and katydids are supposed, by some, to dream.
lines.author: Shirley Jackson
lines.what_its_doing: Jackson opens with a philosophical claim about the human mind's relationship to reality, and then immediately illustrates it with larks and katydids dreaming. The logic is strange on purpose. She says no living organism can exist sanely under conditions of absolute reality, and then offers insects as evidence. The sentence is not about Hill House yet. It's about the psychological necessity of unreality, of dream, of story, of not-quite-seeing, as a survival mechanism. The whole novel is going to argue that Eleanor's instability isn't pathology but an extreme version of a universal need. Hill House preys on that need. Jackson's first sentence says: before you judge Eleanor, understand that what she's doing is what every living thing does. She's just doing it more.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Opening with a psychological or philosophical claim that the rest of the novel will test allows you to set up your character's central vulnerability before the character appears, so the reader arrives with a framework instead of a judgment.

lines.line: My name is Mary Katherine Blackwood.
lines.book: We Have Always Lived in the Castle
lines.author: Shirley Jackson
lines.what_its_doing: On the surface this reads like a mirror of 'My name is Kathy H.', a woman introducing herself by name in first person. The difference is the name itself. Mary Katherine Blackwood is formal, Catholic, old-fashioned, and slightly heavy. Jackson gives her narrator a name that sounds like it belongs on a church registry or a family gravestone. By the end of the first page we'll learn that Mary Katherine dislikes most people and prefers living with her cat on the family estate to any interaction with the village nearby. That name, not 'Kate,' not 'Kathie,' but the full 'Mary Katherine,' tells you before any of that who she is: someone who holds herself at a formal distance, who insists on the full thing, who will not be abbreviated.
lines.what_you_can_steal: A narrator's full formal name as the first three words can carry class, psychology, and social positioning that would take a paragraph of description to convey any other way.

lines.line: It seems increasingly likely that I really will undertake the expedition that has been preoccupying my imagination now for some days.
lines.author: Kazuo Ishiguro
lines.what_its_doing: Ishiguro gives Stevens so many qualifiers in the first sentence that the uncertainty becomes the character. 'It seems increasingly likely,' already hedged. 'That I really will,' the 'really' defensive, as if he's surprised at himself. 'Undertake the expedition that has been preoccupying my imagination now for some days.' Not a trip. An expedition. And it's been 'preoccupying' his imagination, not exciting or worrying him. Preoccupying implies the thought is getting in the way of other things. Stevens is a man who has organized his entire life around emotional suppression, professional duty, and the avoidance of anything resembling personal desire. The first sentence makes you feel all of that in the way he can't bring himself to simply say: I've been thinking about going to see her.
lines.what_you_can_steal: A narrator's over-qualification of a simple desire, the hedges, the formal vocabulary, the excessive precision about duration, can reveal repression more efficiently than any amount of backstory.

lines.line: First the colors.
lines.author: Markus Zusak
lines.what_its_doing: Three words. No article, no verb, no subject. Death is narrating The Book Thief, and the first thing Death notices, wants you to notice, is color. Colors are what Death uses to cope, to process, to stay sane while collecting souls during World War II. The fragment is the right sentence structure for this narrator because Death doesn't experience time or causation the way humans do. It doesn't move through a scene; it notices. 'First the colors' implies a sequence, a priority, a way of seeing that will be established before anything else. It's also a trap: you expect a horror story about World War II and Death gives you colors first. The whole book is built on that displacement: finding beauty inside catastrophe, and asking what that says about survival.
lines.what_you_can_steal: If your narrator has an unusual psychology, let the first sentence model how they perceive the world rather than introducing them by name or situation. The perception is the character.

lines.line: I became what I am today at the age of twelve, on a frigid overcast day in the winter of 1975.
lines.author: Khaled Hosseini
lines.what_its_doing: Hosseini opens on transformation, 'I became what I am today,' and then immediately anchors that transformation to a specific date. The construction is a confession. The narrator is telling you he was shaped by something that happened when he was twelve, in winter, in 1975, and the precision of the details signals that he has been over this moment many times. He knows the date the way people know the dates of accidents or deaths, because he has rehearsed it. The phrase 'what I am today' withholds the definition entirely. You don't know what he is, only that something made him into it, and that the making happened on a specific cold day in a specific year. The entire first chapter builds toward that afternoon, and the whole novel is an attempt to undo it.
lines.what_you_can_steal: Announcing that a specific past moment created who your narrator is, without revealing what that moment was, generates a gravitational pull toward the reveal that can sustain an entire opening chapter.
